SUE Design Manager User Guide

Chapter 3

Properties And Generators

Parameterized Icons

SUE provides a simple, graphical means of creating simple generators (called parameterized icons). This mechanism allows any user to add user definable properties to icons by simply adding special text lines to the icon. Just push into any of the included icons to see examples of how this is done.

Parameterized icons are restricted to only being able to change the text displayed in an instantiated icon and pass properties to the netlister, as a function of changing parameter values. You can't make structural changes to the icons such as adding or deleting I/O's or change the icon shape. If you need the additional features, you need to build REAL SUE generators (see below) in which you write a Tcl program to build an icon/schematic from the parameters given. For example, If you wanted to be able to have an icon property -- say fanin -- that changed a two input nand gate into a three or higher input nand gate, then you need to write a generator.

Defining Properties

Defining parameters in cells and telling SUE how to netlist them is as easy as adding text to the icon view of the cell. Any text in an icon view of a cell that doesn't start with a dash (-) becomes part of the icon "picture" and is displayed when the icon is instantiated into a schematic. Any text starting with a dash is a property definition and is not displayed when the icon is instantiated.

Properties come in five flavors, denoted types, which are: "user", "fixed", "auto", "text", and "comment". Text properties are the default. User properties will appear in the Property Edit menu of an instantiated icon. To define a new user property, simply add the following text line to an icon: 

      -type user -name <name of property> [-default <default value for prop.>] 
      [-choices {[radio|choice|popup|binary] <choice1> <choice2> ...}] 
     

If the default value is "" (in other words, the empty list, or null) then the -default ... string can be omitted. The optional choices keyword allows you to help the user by providing a list of choices for the option. For example, if you wanted to make an nfet icon and give the user a choice of three different SPICE models, you might add the following property: 

      -type user -name model -default n -choices {n n_io nlv} 
      
     

The exact behavior of this property depends on the setting of the SUE variable DEFAULT_PROP_MENU_TYPE which is set in the .suerc file. This variable can be either radio, choice, or popup, with the following results:

  1. radio - provides a set of radio buttons for the user to click. No other choices are possible.

  2. popup - provides the list of choices that the user can click on and choose between OR the user can add their own value.

  3. choice - is like popup but the user is restricted to the choices provided.

If you want a specific behavior, just add the behavior to the beginning of the list of choices. Don't worry, the behavior won't show up as a choice. For example, if you wanted the user to see the nfet models as radio buttons, just modify the above line to be: 

      -type user -name model -default n -choices {radio n n_io nlv} 
      
     

The final type of behavior is called binary. This behavior is useful if a property only has two choices: 1 (on) or 0 (off). This can't be the default behavior since it is restricted to either on or off. If you have a property called verbose, for example, you might use the binary choice: 

      -type user -name verbose -default 0 -choices binary 
      
       
      

      
 SUMMARY:

Text lines in icons are understood to be property definitions if their first character is a "-", so don't start a piece of text with a "-" unless you really want to add a property.

Property definitions are not displayed when the icon is instantiated.

Default Properties in New Icons

When you ask SUE to make a new icon, either by the new icon command in the File menu or by the make other view command in the View menu from a schematic, SUE will automatically add certain default properties to the icon. These defaults are contained in the DEFAULT_PROPERTIES variable in the .suerc file. Typical defaults are for the name, spice "m" or multiplier, and DPC properties, for example: 

      set DEFAULT_PROPERTIES {{-type user -name name} {-type user -name M} {-type user -name dpc}}

Displaying Properties

Once you have defined a property, you can display it with a text string (no "-") which contains the property name prefixed with a "$". So if you created an nfet icon with the properties "W" and "L", you could display them in the icon with, for example, $W/$L. The dollar sign syntax is, surprise, the same syntax which is used in Tcl.

Note that any properties included in the DISPLAY_PROPS variable as set in the .suerc file will automatically be displayed on every instantiated icon. These properties can be displayed in any one of the following locations on the icon:

      • c - the center of the icon

      • ul - the upper left hand corner of the icon

      • ll - the lower left hand corner of the icon

      • ur - the upper right hand corner of the icon

      • lr - the lower right hand corner of the icon

All of these positions are with respect to an icon in the "R0" orientation and rotate and mirror with the icon.

Example: 

      set DISPLAY_PROPS {{name ul} {M ur M=} {dpc ll "dpc "}} 
      
     

will place the icons name (or, the value of its name property) in the upper left hand side of the icon, its "M" property in the upper right prefixed by "M=", etc.

If any of the properties in the DISPLAY_PROPS variable are specifically added to the icon, as for example, $name in the icon view of the cell, then the default placement will be ignored. Thus, if you don't like the automatic placement in only a few cells, you can manually pick a new spot and override it just on those icons. However, you cannot have a property in one place on one instance of an icon and in a different place on a different instance of the same icon.

All text gets run through the Tcl parser and thus we must be careful not to trip over any special Tcl characters in any simple text. The [] (left and right square bracket) characters in Tcl cause evaluation to occur; however, they are commonly used to delimit buses, for example foo[3] or in[31:0] in icons. Therefore, SUE automatically quotes the [] characters to make the common case of buses easier to use. SUE quotes more than just [], it actually quotes the characters "[]{}\ .

Sometimes you really want to do more that just evaluate variables, like calling procedures and evaluating complex expressions. In this case, you must use a slightly more complicated syntax. An example of this is in the nmos icon. We don't want to clutter up our schematics with nmos channel lengths since they are mostly minimum. Thus, we only want to display the channel length if it is different from minimum (which in this example is 0.6µm). So instead of a text line of just $L to display the channel length, we use: 

      -text {[if {$L != "0.6u"} {set L}]} 
      
     

When you use the -text <expression> syntax, SUE will not quote any special characters and thus the Tcl parser can have a field day. For information on how to write crafty Tcl commands to embed into SUE icons, consult the Tcl book or the voluminous Tcl man pages.

If you make a mistake in creating property lines, the entire property will be ignored and a message displayed in the SUE command window when the icon is instantiated into a schematic or if this icon is already instantiated in a schematic when you go to that schematic and the icon must be "remade". Sometimes, the mistake will cause the entire icon to barf. Not to worry, just find your way back to the icon and fix it.

Properties and Netlisting

Parameterized icons are mostly useful when netlisting. For example, you don't just want to define the width (W) and length (L) of an nfet, you also want to pass it to the SPICE netlist. When netlisting, the netlister will first attempt to include the text which corresponds to the NETLIST_PROP in the icon, if it is defined (see Chapter 3, "Netlisting, Simulation and Cross-probing"). Thus, to SPICE netlist the nfet, you might add: 

      -type fixed -name spice -text {[unique_name M $name] $d $g $s gnd $model W=$W L=$L 
      
     

Fixed and auto types are useful for this.

The auto type is special in that it will recreate itself when the icon changes. Auto types are created with create verilog property in the Sim menu. It is presently only defined for the Verilog properties.

Comments

Sometimes you want to remind the user of something only when they edit the icon view of the cell. The comment type is set up for this purpose, for example, the line: 

      -type comment -text {Please don't edit this icon} 
      
     

does nothing (or does it).

Generators

As you've probably figured out by now (especially if you looked at one of the .sue files or carefully read this document), most things like schematics and icons are actually Tcl procedures. Furthermore, the command line (i.e. the window from which you invoked SUE) is a Tcl interpreter. So what are we getting at? You should be able to write generators (i.e. real Tcl programs with loops and expressions, etc.) for icons and schematics. Unfortunately, this does not work transparently because of optimizations in SUE to make icons draw quickly. Remember, much of SUE is done in Tcl which is basically interpreted and (sorry, John) pretty slow. To make the icons draw quickly, SUE "compiles" them into much simpler Tcl code and then executes that code. This breaks generators. However, do not despair because...

Yes, Virginia, there are generators in SUE. A SUE generator takes arguments that can structurally change its icon and schematic (unlike parameterized icons) and create a new icon and schematic. Hence, for every generator, a multitude of cells can be generated, depending on the combinations of its arguments.

The cell with the default arguments has the same name as the .sue file. Others need to have different names. For example, a nand generator might be called nand2, and be in the file nand2.sue, since its default arguments are for 2 inputs. The three input version would be called nand3, despite there not being a file called nand3.sue. This cell is derived from nand2, and if you look into a schematic that instantiates a nand3 icon, you will see that the line: 

      generate nand2 nand3 -ninputs 3 
      
     

must be added before calling any nand3 icons. SUE will automatically add this line.

SUE will attempt to construct a unique name for the newly generated cell from the root of the generator and the concatenation of its non-nil arguments.

Changing generator argument names may cause unforeseen problems because they are referred to in already-existing schematics with the old argument names. Also, rearranging argument names may cause unforseen problems because SUE's unique names are based on the argument names and order.

If you do not like the automatically-created generator name, you can define your own naming procedure for the generator. Just define a procedure called NAME_<generator> which takes the same arguments as the ICON and SCHEMATIC procedures and returns a unique name for that generator given a unique set of arguments.

For example, 

      proc NAME_nor2 args { 
      call_use_keyword $args {{ninputs 2} {name nor2}} 
      return "nor$ninputs" 
      }


This naming procedure must be in the same .sue file as the ICON procedure for its generator or it will be ignored. Also, names should not contain any special characters or spaces.

SUE icon and schematic procedures for non-generators consist of a list of commands (see Chapter 6, SUE File Formats) which each create a single object in the icon and schematic. A generator is a Tcl program which, when executed, must create the same list of commands, but is not limited to just a simple list of those commands. Instead, any valid Tcl program can be written to create those commands, including calling other procedures, reading files, looping, etc. This new icon and schematic then looks exactly like the standard parameterized ones and can be compiled by SUE just the same.

When you make changes to non-generator icons and schematics inside SUE, SUE knows how to recreate their procedures, since they are simply a list of commands. Generators, on the other hand, are derived from possibly complex programs, and hence SUE cannot recreate them. Thus generators cannot be edited inside SUE. If you want to change a specific incantation of the cell (i.e. one with a specific set of arguments), you can SUE copy it to another name, and then modify it and save it out. If you attempt to directly edit a generator cell, SUE will warn you that it is ignoring the changes.

To tell if an instantiated icon is a generator or not, select it and look at the message window. For example, if you select a nand2, you might see: 

      selected: nand2 (generator) R0 #65 
      
     

A generator has two sets of arguments. One set defines its structure, like its number of inputs. The other defines the specific properties of this instance of the icon, as, for example, its name or size. The first, or generator, set of inputs, can be changed by double clicking on this icon while holding the Shift key down. The second, or parameter set, can be changed by simply double-clicking on the icon.

For example, the default cells nor2 and nand2 are both generators. They both have an input called ninputs which can be used to change these gates to have an arbitrary number of inputs. So to create a 4-input CMOS nand gate, Shift-double-click on the nand2 icon in a schematic, then change the ninputs field from 2 to 4, and it is done. Oh, and remember to push into the new icon. You will see that the schematic changed, too!

In order to create an icon generator, you must add the line: 

      icon_generator $args {{ninputs 2}}  
      
     

as the first line of the icon where {{ninputs 2}} should be replaced with a list of lists of argument-default pairs of your choosing.

The associated schematic procedure must be modified from: 

      proc SCHEMATIC_<cell_name> {} {

to: 

      proc SCHEMATIC_<cell_name> args {  
      call_use_keyword $args {{ninputs 2} {name nor2}}  
     

Where {{ninputs 2} {name nor2}} should be replaced with any arguments that need to be used in the schematic. Don't forget the "args" in the procedure definition. Look at the nand2 and nor2 examples if you are considering making your own generators. Good luck.
